title: Miami, FSU among ACC teams asking Congress to change Protect College Sports Act
description: Four teams asked House leaders to allow for more teams in conference realignment than allowed in the Protect College Sports Act the Senate passed.
fullText:
It takes a lot for Florida State and Miami to come together on anything. But leaders from the two bitter rivals signed onto a letter sent to congressional leaders seeking changes to the Protect College Sports Act that would make it easier for the two to potentially leave the ACC and join another power conference.

Presidents and chancellors of UM, FSU, Clemson and North Carolina signed a letter directed to House Speaker Mike Johnson, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and House Majority Whip Tom Emmer requesting an increase in the cap on teams allowed in each conference from 20 to 22. The letter also requests eliminated the requirement that all teams seeking to switch conferences first spend three years as an independent.

"The three-year independence requirement would impose a significant additional consequence on an institution seeking to change conferences, particularly when conferences and their members have already negotiated the financial terms surrounding an exit," the letter states.

Game updates: Follow the latest as Florida State hosts Virginia

"Similarly, a conference membership cap of 20 could unnecessarily constrain future conference configurations and limit important market considerations in potential national media level negotiations."

The letter is signed by FSU President Richard McCullough, Miami President and CEO Joe Echevarria, Clemson President Benjamin C. Ayers and North Carolina Chancellor Lee H. Roberts. It was first reported by Tomahawk Nation.

The desires of each school that signed onto the letter are speculative at this point, though it has been long feared that college sports is heading toward a future in which all the major teams are grouped into two super-conferences: the Big Ten and the SEC. In the multibillion-dollar world of college football, those two conferences have fielded the national champion in seven straight years and 10 of the 12 years of the College Football Playoff. Clemson's wins in 2017 and 2019 are the only ones by a school from another conference, though Miami and part-time ACC team Notre Dame (independent in football) were the past two runners-up.

This is not the first time ACC rivals have come together on the subject of conference realignment. FSU and Clemson independently sued the ACC in 2023 over the conference's media-rights package and the reported $500 million fee required to exit the conference. Both schools settled their lawsuits in 2025 after a new distribution deal was signed.

Coincidentally, the No. 4 Miami football team traveled to face Clemson the night after the letter became public.

The bill passed the Senate on Monday, Sept. 28, as industry leaders seek to rein in what they see as a Wild West landscape of college sports since players gained the ability to freely transfer between schools; make money from name, image and likeness contracts; and remain eligible well past the four years that had been the NCAA standard thanks to injury and COVID exemptions.

The past few months have seen legislators go back and forth with conference leaders and schools to iron out a new set of laws to turn college sports into a tax-exempt model similar to that of professional sports. As part of that discussion, pushback from Florida senators Ashley Moody and Rick Scott kept it from advancing in its early stages. At that time, the provision to cap conference making $700 million annually limited them to 19 teams, while teams seeking to change would have to spend six years as an independent. Moody changed her vote after the limits were raised to 20 teams with a three-year independence requirement.

The PCSA needs a simple majority vote from the House before it goes to President Donald Trump, who has expressed an eagerness to sign it. The House is in recess until after the midterm elections Nov. 3, and even then, the PCSA is not expected to be a top-of-the-line measure.

Despite the constant dialogue between lawmakers, media executives, conference heads and former coaches and athletes, current players have completely been left out of the conversation as to how they will be able to navigate their sports going forward.

fullText:
Eli Manning took the Arch Manning question on The Colin Cowherd Podcast, in an episode released on Thursday, Oct. 1, with his nephew four games into his second season as Texas' starting quarterback. Eli skipped the timeline and described what the Mannings have always expected to get out of college, a standard the family's own history has already tested.

Arch redshirted as a freshman in 2023, so he is a redshirt junior this fall with the 2027 season still available. He can declare for the 2027 NFL Draft after this season or play one more year in Austin and enter the 2028 draft.

Peyton Manning faced a version of that choice after the 1996 season, when he was widely viewed as the likely No. 1 pick, and went back to Tennessee anyway. "I didn't want to be 50 years old wondering what my senior year in college would have been like," Peyton said. That December, he threw for 373 yards and four touchdowns as the Vols came back to beat Auburn 30-29 in the SEC Championship Game, and he went first overall in 1998.

Eli redshirted at Ole Miss and still started four seasons before going first overall in 2004. Archie Manning played out his eligibility at Ole Miss before going second overall in 1971. In 2025, Archie said Arch would not enter the 2026 draft, which held up when Arch returned for this season. Asked about Arch now, Eli described the same approach.

"Yeah, that's the whole point of college, to enjoy being in college, to get better every year. It's opportunities to play more games, to get better, to get more prepared for the NFL. To try to win a national championship or an SEC championship, to be a captain of the team. Like, all those things were important to us," Eli said on The Colin Cowherd Podcast.

"It's not just about, hey, this is all about getting through the NFL and going to the next step. No, it's about enjoying your experience, enjoying your teammates, becoming a better player, becoming a better leader, building something special with the guys that have all been there together. So I'm proud of Arch and how he's handled this and his mindset," Eli added.

Former New York Giants QB Eli Manning seemingly confirmed that his nephew and Texas Longhorns QB Arch Manning is at least considering returning to college for one more season and declaring for the NFL Draft in 2028.

Arch is currently going through his second season as the… pic.twitter.com/IvhvC0M6Vb

— NFL Rumors (@nflrums) October 3, 2026

Arch's first full season as the starter in 2025 produced a 9-3 regular season and a 41-27 bowl win over Michigan, but no SEC title. No Manning has won a national championship, and Peyton remains the only one with an SEC crown. Texas was 4-0 after its Sept. 26 win at Tennessee, so the chase Eli described is open right now.

Arch reportedly made $6.5 million in NIL money in 2024. His uncles played college football long before players could collect anything like it, so another year at Texas costs Arch far less than it would have cost them.

Eli never said which draft Arch will enter, and Arch has not announced anything. The decision waits on a season that is barely a month old.

title: Notre Dame Nabs Six Spots on Early NFL Draft Board
description: For decades, major football programs such as the Notre Dame Fighting Irish have spent heavily on training centers and experienced coaching staffs. Those resources help high school recruits become stronger and more prepared early in their college careers. Top universities now run football programs that work much like professional teams. Scouts follow talented college players […] The post Notre Dame Nabs Six Spots on Early NFL Draft Board appeared first on Gridiron Heroics.
fullText:
For decades, major football programs such as the Notre Dame Fighting Irish have spent heavily on training centers and experienced coaching staffs. Those resources help high school recruits become stronger and more prepared early in their college careers.

Top universities now run football programs that work much like professional teams. Scouts follow talented college players for years, while fans pay close attention to young players with strong physical skills.

On Thursday, sports media ESPN published its early player rankings for the 2027 professional football draft. Industry analyst Jordan Reid evaluated college athletes across the nation and selected six Notre Dame players for his top 50 list.

Leading this collegiate group, junior cornerback Leonard Moore earned the second overall spot. Reid wrote, "With excellent length, speed and technique, Moore is the prototypical cornerback prospect."

Because Moore allowed zero completed passes through late September, scouts consider him an elite defender. Furthermore, his teammate CJ Carr ranked 22nd on the national list after throwing for 963 yards and nine touchdowns.

Reid praised the young quarterback in his report, stating that Carr is a "refined pocket passer whose eyes, feet and throwing motion are always in cohesion." Consequently, Carr's accurate passing numbers elevated his status among professional evaluators.

Four additional Notre Dame athletes rounded out the prestigious board. Specifically, safety Brauntae Johnson earned the 26th position.

Subsequently, edge rusher Boubacar Traore secured spot 47 after producing 2.5 sacks this autumn. Linebacker Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa was selected 48th.

Finally, offensive lineman Anthonie Knapp grabbed the 49th rank because he surrendered only a 0.9 percent pressure rate on 230 snaps.

NFL rules require players to be at least three years removed from high school before entering the draft. True juniors and redshirt sophomores may qualify, but true freshmen and true sophomores cannot declare before completing that waiting period.

The rule prevents true college sophomores from signing NFL contracts before the 2027 draft. An early ESPN ranking gives a player attention, but it does not offer a contract or guarantee any money.

NFL teams make their own decisions during the scouting process. They study game film, conduct medical checks and watch players complete athletic drills before making draft selections.

Strong media rankings can still bring national attention to a college program. However, NFL scouts follow their own watchlists and attend practices and games based on each team's evaluation plans.

Six Notre Dame players included in early media rankings are still college students. They remain active members of the team during the current season.

title: 'Let me clarify': John Calipari backtracks after controversial press conference
description: The legendary college coach made a correction.
fullText:
'Let me clarify': John Calipari backtracks after controversial press conference originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

John Calipari felt like he needed to add a bit of context to previous comments he made on Wednesday. After making remarks about player compensation and the Protect College Sports Act that went viral, the Arkansas Razorbacks basketball coach took to social media on Friday to explain his position.

Calipari wanted to clear the air and make sure everyone knew he was not against players getting paid. This is a complete reversal of what he said less than 48 hours prior.

"I did a press conference two days ago. Let me clarify what I said," Calipari wrote. "I've always been about the players and what benefits them my entire career."

He went on to write, "I am GREAT with my guys making money and want them to make even more money. And they deserve all the advantages that come along with playing college sports."

Calipari provided his thoughts on the current state of college athletics and his support for the PCSA. Despite his best efforts to not say we should turn the clock back, he alluded to players getting paid and needing to be secondary.

"Right now, we need something to give us some semblance of order and some guardrails," Calipari stated on Wednesday. "I'm going to say this. I probably shouldn't. Nine of my players make more than my assistants. And the other three make more than all my staff. And we are not one of the highest payers. We're just not."

Those comments became part of a bigger conversation as the U.S. Senate passed PCSA. The topic of player compensation, coaching salaries and the future structure of college sports are all hanging in the balance. Calipari is one of a thousand voices, but he's always been one of the loudest. After making $125 million in his career, I guess he forgot what capitalism looks like.

That appears to be the point Calipari wants to ditch. We'll see if PCSA becomes law or not. For now, player should fight for every protection possible. Otherwise, coaches like Calipari will try to dismantle anything they've built brick by brick.

title: Inside Northern Ireland's football conveyor belt
description: BBC Sport NI spends the day at the IFA JD Academy Residential at Campbell College where Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill catches up with the young players hoping to graduate to a full-time career.
fullText:
Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill has made no bones about his desire to give youth a chance.

Included in the squad this international window are teenagers Ceadach O'Neill, Tom Atcheson, Braiden Graham and Kieran Morrison, while 21-year-old Patrick Kelly and 22-year-old Terry Devlin have begun to stake their claim for regular inclusion.

A golden generation, or is this simply Northern Ireland's football factory - the IFA JD National Academy - beginning to bear fruit?

As Northern Ireland fans began to digest Monday's 0-0 draw at home to Hungary, following a 1-0 win in Georgia on Friday which has ensured a positive start to their Nations League campaign, O'Neill visited Campbell College which is home to the academy where teenage hopefuls seek to develop into potential stars at club and international level.

"I know about all these players in here, know the clubs they are attracting attention from, their positions," O'Neill told BBC Sport NI.

"We have regular meetings as staff every month with regular updates on the academy and where those players are going.

"Our job is to prepare them as best as possible and guide them if that opportunity comes to take the next step into the professional game in England or Scotland."

The academy at Campbell College is a residential, designed for 24 elite young players at under-15 and under-16 level, providing preparation for life away from home should that come to pass.

While athletes, they remain students with equal emphasis on football and life skills. Education in the classroom is a key component because, in the world of professional football, there are no guarantees.

Academy student Bailey Magee plays at club level with Glenavon.

His day is typical for a 16-year-old with school dominating until mid-afternoon. Once the bell rings, however, it is time to hit the gym and the pitch before returning to any school work in the evening.

If his dream of becoming a professional footballer comes true, then spending so much time away from home will be worth it.

"Going away with Northern Ireland has helped me because I'm able to stay away from home and you get used to that a wee bit," said Magee.

"The hardest times are [after] Christmas because that's when you're coming back after spending a long time with family.

"The IFA and Campbell have done really well when you're trying to mix the two and balance football with studies.

"I'll work hard until the end of the year and whatever happens, happens. I'll maybe do A-Levels, maybe a B.Tech or full-time football academy with the likes of Linfield or Larne, so there are loads of different pathways for us."

Those sentiments are shared by 15-year-old Kayson Braniff who is currently on the books at Linfield.

"My dad had drilled it into my head that we need our studies," he said.

"It's not as if football is everything, studies come first because you definitely need them in case football doesn't work out."

Clubs in England have the ability to integrate young players into their systems from a young age, which can mean those from NI playing catch-up if and when they make the switch in their mid-teens.

Therefore, preparing potential stars for the rigours of life in a new environment with new coaches can only be enhanced by time in the NI academy which O'Neill believes makes teenagers "better equipped" to make their mark at an English or Scottish club.

Helping young players realise their professional dream is intrinsic, but for Northern Ireland, unearthing new stars to graduate into the senior team is equally important.

"Two or three years ago we brought players in a bit younger than their club career suggested they were at that level, but it pays dividends now," said the current boss.

"You need the right people in the right positions to make that work and I think we have that.

"Players have decisions to make on their club situations and international situations, but your pathway is very important as it builds a loyalty within players.

"We want young players from whatever part of the community they come from to be part of this pathway to become senior international players."

Pathways are all well and good, but watching previous graduates from the academy go on to wear the green jersey or star in Champions League games like Conor Bradley ensures it is a tangible goal for those currently involved.

The current Northern Ireland manager taking such an active interest helps too.

"He's a really nice guy and to think I could be in that team in the next few years, which is the goal, it's really reassuring," Magee said of his sitdown with O'Neill on Tuesday.

Braniff agreed O'Neill's interest confirms "he cares about the youth".

Both are hopeful they can follow in the footsteps of previous graduates. If that results in a move to a full-time club, it will represent another success story for the academy.

"It doesn't matter who it's for or where it is, so long as it's a professional team and a professional contract," said Braniff.

title: Boston College Football vs. SMU: Betting Preview & Prediction
description: After last week’s fourth-quarter meltdown against Virginia Tech, Boston College is back in action on the road against SMU. After covering last week’s 14.5-point spread against the Hokies, BC rolls into Dallas as 20.5 point dogs. Simply put: I’m not feeling great about this one.
fullText:
After last week's fourth-quarter meltdown against Virginia Tech, Boston College is back in action on the road against SMU. After covering last week's 14.5-point spread against the Hokies, BC rolls into Dallas as 20.5 point dogs.

Simply put: I'm not feeling great about this one. I know BC covered against Tech and arguably should have emerged with a win, but I think there are several mitigating factors that suggest SMU is the play here. Firstly, the nor'easter without a doubt benefited BC. Ethan Grunkemeyer never really looked comfortable until the fourth quarter, keeping the Hokies' offense largely one-dimensional for much of the game. Comparatively, BC's offense never really wanted to throw the ball anyways, and McKenzie's legs offered a consistent outlet. The weather essentially played right into BC's preferred style of play while limiting the Hokies. Even with some rain scheduled for Saturday, there's no way conditions in Dallas on Saturday—in particular the wind—are as severe as they were in Chestnut Hill last week. That hurts the Eagles.

Secondly, Boston College's offense looks more one-dimensional than ever right now. The only reason BC was able to move the chains last week was the QB run game. At some point, teams are simply gonna abandon rushing the passer in favor of flooding the backfield with defenders and containing McKenzie in the pocket. They are going to make the Eagles offense win through the air, and the Eagles have not shown they can do that yet.

Thirdly, Coach O'Brien mentioned in his weekly presser that a flu-like illness is ripping through the team. Impact guys like Demetrius Ballard barely played last week, and presumably the roster will be thinned by whatever ailment is plaguing the team. Injuries have also continued to take their toll on the Eagles; Syair Torrence is still not fully healthy, while Bodie Kahoun is still out and Kris Jones aggravated an ankle injury last week.

Between the return of normal weather, BC's offensive struggles, and the team availability issues, I'm backing the Mustangs—especially when you consider the fact that Kevin Jennings is still somehow on the team.

title: Rape case at Cornell turns spotlight on campus sexual assault
description:
The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, on September 28, 2026. - Heather Ainsworth/AP
It was 7:05 p.m. on a Wednesday in mid-September when Jane Doe’s lawsuit hit the New York County Supreme Court docket. Within days, the 101-page, double-spaced filing had captured the nation’s attention, sparking outrage and controversy and refocusing attention on a longstanding issue: sexual assault on college campus.
fullText:
It was 7:05 p.m. on a Wednesday in mid-September when Jane Doe’s lawsuit hit the New York County Supreme Court docket. Within days, the 101-page, double-spaced filing had captured the nation’s attention, sparking outrage and controversy and refocusing attention on a longstanding issue: sexual assault on college campus.

The complaint was explosive, claiming that seven members of a Cornell University fraternity took part in the sexual assault of a 20-year-old sorority member during a drug-fueled, hours-long encounter in the fall of 2024. Included in the filing was a screenshot of a Snapchat message where one of the men wrote that there was “free p*ssy” and others responded gleefully, with comments like “CHI PHIII.”

Soon after the lawsuit’s filing on Sept. 16, a familiar pattern played out. Furious onlookers took to social media to demand accountability, flooded the district attorney’s office with complaints and shared photos and other identifying details of the fraternity members many have taken to calling “the Cornell 7.” Others, meanwhile, condemned the rush to judgment or urged caution in drawing conclusions from the allegations in the lawsuit, which a prosecutor said differ from what the alleged victim reported in 2024. Some hurried to try to unmask the anonymous woman behind the accusations.

There were flashes of politics and victim blaming, judgment and shame in a case that’s rife with unanswered questions and likely to evolve as more details come to light.

The issue of sexual assault on campus – and how allegations should be handled – has resurfaced again and again. An individual case grabs the attention of the nation and sets off a debate over where we are as a country and whether change is needed: Columbia University student Emma Sulkowicz carrying a mattress to protest how her report was handled; Chanel Miller delivering a fiery victim impact statement at the sentencing of a former Stanford University swimmer convicted of assaulting her; Summer Willis crawling to the Texas state capitol on her hands and knees to secure a change to the legal loophole that allowed her assault to go unprosecuted.

Social media posts by actresses Florence Pugh and Mariska Hargitay helped move the Cornell conversation forward, gathering steam as commentary about the case flooded feeds.

Sasha Pieterse, an actress known for her starring role in the hit show “Pretty Little Liars,” told CNN she herself is a survivor of sexual assault. It’s something she has not publicly spoken about until now.

Pieterse said she does not think people “understand the gravity of what happens around the aftermath: the fear, the shame, the level of physical and mental recovery.”

She said she hopes the spotlight on the Cornell allegations will help other victims feel less alone and show why consent laws should be standardized.

“I never want anything like what just happened at Cornell to happen to any other person,” Pieterse said.

Laura L. Dunn, a victims’ rights attorney with a specialization in campus assault cases, heard about the Cornell case almost immediately after the complaint was filed. People across her life sent it to her, reminded not only of her efforts to address the issue but also of her own personal connection to it: As a student athlete on the University of Wisconsin at Madison’s crew team in 2004, she reported being assaulted by two male teammates. No charges were filed.

“It’s a very painful moment in time, on many levels, to see a case that I could have read about 20 years ago happening again,” said Dunn, 41.

Attorneys for two of the seven alleged assailants at Cornell have denied the allegations and some observers have argued that what happened that night in 2024 did not qualify as a crime under New York law – a comment that has also been made by Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten in defending his decision not to file criminal charges when the incident was reported. He said the alleged victim at the time described “her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual.”

Van Houten said this week he will reopen the case, adding that he recognizes “the reality that it can take years of therapy and healing for victims of sexual assaults to fully process and understand what happened to them.”

Others online have tried to tie the Cornell case to high profile incidents that were determined to be unfounded and the alleged perpetrators wrongly accused, such as cases involving Duke University lacrosse players and a fraternity at the University of Virginia that was the subject of a retracted Rolling Stone article.

Research has found that false allegations are rare, estimated to represent 2 to 10 percent of reports, according to one analysis.

After her own assault, Dunn vowed to push for change – and felt in the 2010s that major progress was being made. A high point for her came in 2011, when the Obama administration reminded higher education institutions of their obligation under Title IX to address sexual violence and directed them to step up their investigations into reports.

Colleges and universities responded, she said, by doing more meaningful educational efforts and boosting their Title IX offices.

“There were all these efforts during that era to really turn the tide,” Dunn said.

More people began speaking out, and by 2014 several high-profile incidents – including Emma Sulkowicz’s – held the public’s interest and drove a desire for change. At the same time, some critics worried that the Obama-era guidance had gone too far, tasking college bureaucrats with investigating criminal allegations and diluting due process.

The first Trump administration withdrew it in 2017, citing concerns about due process. Title IX protections were expanded again under rules set by the Biden administration’s Department of Education, which survivor advocates said removed some of the barriers faced by victims of sexual assault. Those changes were again undone this week by Trump officials.

The move cements a change the Trump administration had informally enacted last year to the federal law banning discrimination based on sex and governs how schools respond to complaints of sexual misconduct. The 2020 guidance narrowed the definition of sexual harassment, extended protections for students accused of sexual misconduct and added requirements like live hearings with the potential for cross-examination.

Emma Grasso Levine, a grad student and senior manager of Title IX policy and programs at Advocates for Youth, told CNN the move “sends a message that it’s not safe to speak out.”

Activists say recent years have seen a backlash to the Me Too movement, coupled with the rise of the “manosphere,” both of which have contributed to the climate around sexual assault on college campuses. National Organization for Women president Kim Villanueva described the content as often promoting women as objects and encouraging or glorifying rape culture.

Her team has been having conversations with college students about the Cornell investigation and the meaning of consent. She said it’s important to have conversations with young men about consent and how they view women in society.

“It will involve a lot of social change,” Villanueva said.

Saanya Agarwal was a sophomore at Cornell in 2024 when the university sent an alert about a reported sexual assault on campus. She remembers it mentioned several men allegedly being involved but that it was otherwise scarce on details – something she found unnerving as a female student sharing a campus with them.

Now a senior, she told CNN that her anger at what she considered a lack of transparency fueled her run for a student assembly position representing women. She was elected and spent last year talking to university administrators and Greek life representatives to try to advocate for more transparency.

“I think if you talk to people, especially women on campus, this question is always in the back of your head: What if that was me?” said Agarwal, who is a sorority member.

Reyes Almeida, a junior at Boston University, said the Cornell incident is appalling, but didn’t surprise her because of how “pervasive” sexual assault is on college campuses.

Almeida is president of BU’s chapter of ‘It’s On Us,’ an organization that supports sexual assault survivors on college campuses and tries to prevent assaults from happening through intervention training.

Many of the survivors their organization works with have chosen not to report their sexual assault to the university, Almeida said. CNN has reached out to BU about survivors choosing not to report assault.

Her opinion is that some universities prioritize image over safety. “The only thing they want to do is keep their pristine image,” Almeida said.

At Rowan University, like others around the country, students receive notification when there is a reported sexual assault on campus in compliance with the federal Clery Act.

Tamyah Crafton, a college senior who founded Rowan University’s chapter of the National Council of Negro Women, appreciates these notifications, but wants more information surrounding them and town hall meetings to discuss the details.

“Like, what are you doing to make the campus safer?” Crafton asked.

At Cornell, administrators barred Chi Phi from campus and launched a task force on sexual assault, which issued recommendations earlier this year.

But Agarwal, the Cornell student, said the perceived lack of transparency from Cornell leaves students to wonder about exactly what happened – and whether someone involved might be sitting next to them in class or across from them at the local bar.

“There’s so much distrust and that also creates fear, understandably so, because we don’t know what’s going on,” she said.

CNN’s Jason Carroll and Linh Tran contributed to this report.

fullText:
Deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence have become a point of deep concern for legislators, advocates and the public

An image of College Park, Georgia mayor Bianca Motley Broom kissing a man – who was not her husband – in a bar spread far and wide on Facebook. The fact that it’s fake is spreading faster, now, but only after it had been seen by thousands of people.

“I think this is a sad commentary about where we are in our democracy, and where we are in our political discourse,” Motley Broom said. “It also seeks to reinforce really tired stereotypes about women in leadership.”

Six years ago, when Motley Broom first took office in the Atlanta suburb, a political enemy might have needed at least rudimentary skill with image-editing software to forge an image of a politician in a compromising position. Today, all that is required is a computer and a prompt for an AI image generator.

The threat of deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence has become a point of deep concern by legislators, advocates and the public.

A poll taken mid-June by Rad Campaign, a digital marketing agency, and Women Who Tech, an advocacy organization for female entrepreneurs, showed that about 71% of respondents worry about AI-generated deepfakes and disinformation affecting elections, while two in three respondents said they were concerned about AI being used to sexualize women.

“The findings show that Americans are more concerned about AI’s use in deepfakes, election disinformation, and the sexualization of women and children than its impact on jobs or the economy,” said Allyson Kapin, founder of the Rad Campaign and cofounder of Women Who Tech.

The Trump administration has a penchant for deploying AI imagery. In January, the White House’s official account on the social media platform X posted a digitally altered image of Nekima Levy Armstrong, who had been arrested in connection with a demonstration that disrupted church services in St Paul, Minnesota.

A picture of her calmly being escorted by a DHS agent was altered so that she appeared to be crying, and her skin had been darkened. Kaelan Dorr, the White House deputy communications director, later described the image as a “meme”.

Fake images of Zohran Mamdami, New York’s mayor, also began circulating from a “parody” account on X in February, falsely depicting him and his mother in the company of disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. Using Google’s SynthID tool, Reuters debunked the images, but not before other accounts had recirculated them as authentic, fueling conspiracy theories.

Despite significant apprehension around the potential economic consequences of AI, concern about deepfake images being used to sexualize women or children, or to influence elections, outstrips concern about AI affecting jobs by about three to one, Kapin said.

“The public is deeply concerned.”

Raphael Warnock, a Georgia Democratic senator, said in a video posted to Facebook that deepfake images had been circulating online falsely depicting him with health problems, with an armful of grandchildren he does not have – and with a full head of hair, which he said was funny, if problematic.

“As these tools become increasingly powerful, it will get harder and harder to distinguish fact from fiction, and there are already bad actors out there, who are doing everything they can to divide us and confuse us,” Warnock said. “This has huge implications for our democracy. What if hours before an election, someone created a page with AI, generated images, fake stories about the candidates, how will voters know what’s true, and what’s not true?”

Warnock is among a group of senate Democrats who have been war-gaming political responses to possible election interference scenarios. Chief among those scenarios: disinformation driven by fabricated images or videos circulated through social media.

Outgoing US senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, offered a bill last week requiring AI firms to install a “kill switch” for rogue AI. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky blocked Kennedy’s bill, describing the effort as premature without additional industry input.

Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic House minority leader, said in an interview earlier this month on SiriusXM that government should move “urgently” on AI regulations, broadly, calling for “guardrails to protect the American people from bad actors and bad behavior”, adding: “It should be a high priority.”

Jeffries noted that Republicans attempted to pass legislation preempting states from regulating AI last year, as part of the omnibus One Big Beautiful Bill. The amendment failed on a 99-1 vote in the senate.

State legislatures are also wrestling with AI regulation amid a widespread, bipartisan public backlash. Some states have legislation like Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security Act – the Elvis Act – which protects politicians and residents alike from AI voice cloning and digital likeness replication, using the state’s robust right-of-publicity protections that are a product of Nashville’s recording industry.

Clear disclaimers are legally required in most states when a political campaign uses AI to manipulate the speeches, appearances or actions of officials or candidates. Georgia is not one of them.

While legislators in Georgia began debated deepfake protections in bills proposed in 2024 and 2025, they have not yet enacted legislation.

Motley Broom said she believes she was targeted by political opponents who objected to her role as a past president of the Georgia Municipal Association. “I have worked for my city to try to be the best advocate I can be on behalf of College Park,” Motley Broom said. “And I certainly won’t be deterred by internet trolls who think this carries weight.”

While she could consider legal action under existing defamation law in Georgia, Motley Broom paused for a moment when asked what legislators should be doing about this. The first amendment protection for speech has to be considered, she said.

“These types of attacks should not be without consequences,” she said. “I hope that lawmakers can address this in a way that balances not only first amendment protections, but the right of an individual not to have completely false accusations being levied. And I’m really hopeful that … that lawmakers on the state and federal level can think about that and think about it carefully, because this is the tip of the iceberg.”

title: The 3 most surprising teams of the college football season
description: The college football season is always full of surprises, and a few weeks into the season, it’s safe to say that a few teams have already delivered. fullText:
The college football season is always full of surprises, and a few weeks into the season, it's safe to say that a few teams have already delivered.

There have already been a handful of teams that have simply not lived up to the hype, but there have been a few teams that have already defied even the most optimistic of expectations.

While there's still a lot of season remaining, here are three teams that have gotten off to a surprising start to the 2026 season.

Two years ago, Mississippi State finished with just a 2-10 record, and things didn't get much better the following year, as the Bulldogs finished with just a 5-7 record. Through head coach Jeff Lebby's first two seasons, Mississippi State won just one SEC conference game. This year has already been radically different.

Through the first four weeks of the season, Mississippi State is 4-0 and 2-0 in the SEC after a gutty 31-24 comeback victory over No. 19 Missouri, and they're led by a legitimate Heisman Trophy candidate in Kamario Taylor, who has established himself as one of the best quarterbacks in the country through the first quarter of the regular season.

It's worth noting that Mississippi State did start the 2025 season with a 4-0 record, and those games included a win over No. 12 Arizona State. However, this team feels different in both its identity and talent. But we'll have a good idea of where they really stand next week when they host No. 7 Alabama.

The past two seasons have been rough for the Oklahoma State Cowboys as the team went a combined 4-20 in 2024 and 2025 and hadn't beaten an FBS team since September of 2024. After parting ways with Mike Gundy following last season, the Eric Morris era looked like more of the same in the season-opener as the Cowboys fell 24-10 to Tulsa to start the season.

Since then, however, Oklahoma State has looked like a totally new team, and that began with a stunning win over No. 6 Oregon just a week later. The Cowboys outplayed Oregon from almost start to finish, putting up 554 yards to beat Oregon 39-31, notching the program's first FBS win in two years.

Oklahoma State has kept the same momentum the past two weeks, shutting out Murray State 59-0 before blowing out previously unbeaten West Virginia 41-24 on the road, snapping an 18-game Big 12 losing streak that went all the way back to the 2023 season.

Heading into the season, Oklahoma State was expected to be one of the worst Power 4 teams in the country. Now, just four weeks into the season, the Cowboys are the No. 19 team in the AP Poll.

After firing head coach Bill Napier in the middle of what turned out to be a 4-8 season, the Florida Gators seemed to be headed toward a rebuilding year under new head coach Jon Sumrall. However, four games into the 2026 season, Sumrall has seemingly engineered an instant turnaround.

Florida went 3-0 to start the season, but the statement came this week against No. 4 Ole Miss. Florida rushed for 302 yards and six touchdowns in a 52-28 blowout. The 52 points tied the most Florida has ever scored against a top-five opponent in history with the only other time coming in the 1997 Sugar Bowl, when the Gators won the national championship. This came a week after Ole Miss established itself as a legitimate playoff contender with a win over LSU.

The biggest difference so far has been the offense. The Gators have scored at least 44 points in every game, and Sumrall is the first SEC head coach to score 200 points in his first four games. They've already scored 28 touchdowns, one shy of their total from all of last season.

The schedule doesn't get easier, with Missouri, Texas, and Georgia all coming in October. But after years of mediocrity in Gainesville, Florida suddenly looks like a real threat in the SEC and in the College Football Playoff race.

title: Senate passes the Protect College Sports Act
description: Report says there's a "0.0 percent chance" the House passes it before election day in November.
fullText:
Big-time college sports has moved halfway toward the federal bailout they crave. The rest of the journey is unlikely to happen soon.

The U.S. Senate passed the so-called "Protect College Sports Act" on Monday night, by a vote of 77-22. The bill now goes to the U.S. House of Representatives.

Earlier in the day, Pat Forde of SI.com cited an unnamed source who said that there is a "0.0 percent chance" the House will pass the bill before the midterm elections.

With the Democrats widely expected to seize control of the House in November, the question then becomes whether it will do any meaningful business before the next Congress convenes in January.

So there's still a long way to go before the NCAA and its members get the antitrust exemption and other benefits designed to stave off a catastrophe. Even as college football is more popular and profitable than ever.

There's chaos, they say. From whose perspective? The players, after years of being exploited by a system that denied them the opportunity to participate meaningfully in the value they generate, are sitting pretty. It's not chaotic for them; it's the free market in operation.

But the schools apparently can't be trusted to balance their budgets, which is bullshit. Every American business faces an ongoing challenge to adapt or fail. In lieu of expecting the administrators to come up with a better way to carve up the pie and/or to spend within their means, they want artificial restrictions on what the players can make.

That's not how it should be. And, despite the Senate vote, maybe it won't be.

title: SEC, power conferences release statements after Protect College Sports Act passes Senate vote

fullText:
After the Protect College Sports Act passed a full Senate vote 77-23 on Monday, each of the power conference released a statement praising the advancement. The bipartisan legislation will now head to the U.S. House of Representatives.

The power conferences all voiced their support for the Protect College Sports Act as it went through the Senate. At first, only the Big 12 and ACC were on board, but the SEC and Big Ten announced their full support in late July to give the bill some momentum. The NCAA also supported it and released its statement shortly after passage.

From there, the bill advanced out of a markup and committee vote, as well as multiple procedural votes. After debate and votes on amendments Monday, the legislation passed the Senate. It will now head to the House, which is not due back in session until after the midterm elections.

"The bipartisan Senate passage of the Protect College Sports Act represents an important step toward establishing a clear and durable national framework for college athletics," the SEC said in its statement. "We look forward to working with members of the House of Representatives to advance legislation that protects student-athletes, provides consistent national standards for universities and conferences, supports women's and Olympic sports, and strengthens the long-term future of college athletics.

"The SEC and our 16 member universities will remain actively and constructively engaged as the legislative process continues, with the goal of achieving a national framework that provides stability, accountability, and clarity for college sports."

In its statement, the Big Ten credited the Senators who sponsored the bill. Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) introduced it in late May, and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) and Chris Coons (D-Del.) joined as co-sponsors.

"We are pleased the Protect College Sports Act has passed the Senate, and are appreciative of the substantial work that has gone into the effort from the act's authors, sponsors, and supporters," the Big Ten's statement read. "We look forward to the next steps to passage as we continue to support the act as passed by the Senate."

Additionally, the Big 12 cited the importance of the Protect College Sports Act's advancement. The conference cited the need to "move beyond uncertainty" as the landscape continues to shift in the NIL and revenue-share eras.

"We are encouraged by the continued progress of the Protect College Sports Act and appreciate the bipartisan leadership of Chairman Cruz, Ranking Member Cantwell, and others that has moved this effort forward," the Big 12's statement read. "The legislation provides a more stable national framework for college athletics, incorporates important transparency measures, and moves our industry closer to a sustainable model that supports student-athletes, institutions, conferences, and fans.

"The future of college sports depends on our ability to move beyond uncertainty and toward lasting solutions, and the Protect College Sports Act is an important step in that direction. We look forward to working with lawmakers as the process advances."

The Protect College Sports Act would grant the NCAA an antitrust exemption to limit athletes to one transfer without penalty, standardize the new five-year, age-based eligibility policy, increase the revenue-sharing cap to nearly $50, put more enforcement in place around the rev-share cap, create an agent registry with a maximum 5% fee and allow schools to pool together their media rights, among other things.

Three amendments were added to the Protect College Sports Act on Monday after the Senate voted on seven of them. One would increase the conference limit to 20 members, rather than the 19 members in the bill's initial text, and another would require schools to disclose foreign funding in college sports. The third would allow states to pass more health and safety requirements through statute and common law.

Up next for the Protect College Sports Act is the House of Representatives. However, the House moved to take two weeks out of its calendar and is not due back until November, after the midterm elections. Cruz has expressed optimism the House will return to vote on the legislation.

Should the bill advance out of the House, it would then head to President Donald Trump's desk. Trump has been a strong supporter of the legislation, and Cruz has suggested he sign it into law on ESPN's College GameDay.

title: How the Protect College Sports Act could affect Charlie Woods and college golf
description: A new Senate bill seeks to stabilize college sports amid NIL chaos, potentially impacting stars like Charlie Woods.
fullText:
TaylorMade's decision to sign Charlie Woods to an NIL deal looked significant when it was announced earlier this month. Now, with federal lawmakers moving closer to reshaping the entire college sports landscape, the agreement may look even more consequential.

The Protect College Sports Act cleared a major hurdle this week after passing the Senate and advancing to the House of Representatives, bringing college athletics a step closer to the most sweeping federal overhaul in years. Supporters say the legislation would bring stability to a system upended by unrestricted player movement, conference realignment and a rapidly evolving name, image and likeness marketplace.

In a 77-22 vote on Capitol Hill on Monday, Sept. 28, the years-long legislative proposal formally cleared its first major hurdle, with eight co-sponsors, headlined by the early work of Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.).

"The most important part of the bill is bringing order to chaos," Cruz told USA TODAY Sports. "College sports is the Wild West. There are essentially no rules. Litigation has struck down virtually all the rules, and as a result, you have athletes going into the transfer portal two, three, four times. You have athletes competing for seven or eight years. You have 27, 28-year-olds competing against 17-year-olds. You have pro players coming back and playing college sports, and every school is in a spending spiral where virtually every athletic department is losing millions of dollars. Many of them are losing tens of millions of dollars. It's unsustainable, and as a consequence, every week we see a different problem.

"Programs being canceled, we see women's sports being canceled. We see Olympic sports being canceled, and if Congress doesn't act within a few years, we will see hundreds of thousands of roster slots and scholarship positions going away, and that would be a tragedy. It would be a tragedy because every year right now we have roughly 500,000 college athletes in America."

For golf, the bill could have far-reaching implications.

When TaylorMade signed Woods, the son of 15-time major champion Tiger Woods, the move underscored how NIL opportunities have expanded beyond traditional revenue sports. Woods, who is committed to Florida State and entering his senior year of high school, became one of the most visible examples of a golfer leveraging his personal brand before arriving on a college campus.

At the time, the agreement signaled more than an equipment partnership. It reflected the growing value of elite amateur golfers as marketing assets. While top junior players have long received free clubs, balls and apparel from manufacturers, paid NIL agreements remain relatively rare in college golf. One Division I men's coach recently estimated that only a few dozen players currently have manufacturer deals that include compensation.

The Protect College Sports Act would not eliminate NIL opportunities such as Woods' partnership with TaylorMade. Athletes would still be free to pursue outside endorsement agreements and marketing relationships. Instead, the legislation seeks to establish a national framework for college athletics while providing additional revenue-sharing opportunities through schools, a move supporters believe would reduce uncertainty for athletes and athletic departments alike.

The bill also includes provisions aimed at protecting Olympic and non-revenue sports, a category that includes golf. Backers argue that without federal intervention, schools facing mounting financial pressure could be forced to reduce scholarships, cut roster spots or eliminate sports. The legislation would allow schools to direct additional revenue-sharing funds toward women's and Olympic sports, a measure supporters say could help preserve opportunities for future golfers.

That matters for players like Woods and the next generation of elite juniors. As NIL has transformed recruiting and athlete compensation, concerns have grown about whether smaller sports could lose ground while schools direct resources toward football and men's basketball. Supporters of the legislation contend that a more structured system could help maintain funding and scholarship opportunities across all sports.

The proposal still faces a vote in the House before it can reach President Donald Trump's desk, but its progress is another sign that the NIL era is entering a new phase.

title: US Senate passes landmark overhaul of college sports

fullText:
The US Senate approved a landmark federal framework for college sports Monday, voting 72-22 to bring order to a multibillion-dollar industry whose biggest events can draw television audiences comparable to major professional championships.

The bipartisan Protect College Sports Act would regulate how universities pay athletes, restrict transfers and give the governing NCAA limited protection from antitrust lawsuits after years of court battles transformed the economics of college athletics.

The vote was one of the Senate's last major legislative acts before lawmakers leave Washington to campaign for the November 3 midterm elections.

The bill now goes to the House of Representatives, which is already in recess until after Election Day, leaving a narrow window for Congress to complete work before a new legislature takes office in January.

President Donald Trump's administration has endorsed the legislation, and the 80-year-old leader himself cheered the bill's passage Monday night, posting to his Truth Social platform that "it will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves."

Unlike university sports in most countries, American college athletics is a vast commercial enterprise.

More than 30 million people watched January's college football national championship on TV while the major conferences -- regional groupings of universities that organize competition and negotiate media rights -- have signed multibillion-dollar broadcasting contracts.

The legislation follows years of upheaval during which athletes won the right to profit from their names and images and, following a 2025 court settlement, universities began paying players directly.

It would establish national rules governing those payments and allow schools to spend nearly $50 million annually through revenue-sharing and other funds.

Athletes would generally be allowed one transfer without sitting out a season, while agents' fees would be capped at five percent.

The bill also provides longer-term scholarship and healthcare protections and seeks to safeguard women's and Olympic sports.

Supporters argue that nationwide rules are needed to replace a patchwork of state laws and repeated litigation.

"Student athletes deserve to get paid. They deserve real protections. And high school athletes deserve a fair shot to compete," said Senator Ted Cruz, who co-sponsored the bill.

"The Protect College Sports Act delivers that while protecting women's and Olympic sports and preserving the game we love for generations to come," the Texas Republican added.

But the measure has divided Democrats and drawn opposition from racial equality activists, labor unions and the Congressional Black Caucus.

Critics say its antitrust protections give too much power back to the NCAA while limiting athletes' legal rights and leaving unresolved whether college players should ultimately be treated as employees entitled to collective bargaining.

The House could seek changes, potentially forcing another Senate vote and complicating efforts to send the legislation to Trump before the current Congress expires.

And the administration has pursued its own definition since President Trump returned to office, making deals with schools such as the University of Pennsylvania to take transgender athletes out of their women’s programs.

Opponents of the move say it will harm transgender athletes and weaken protections for sexual assault victims.

“Sexual harassment and assault continue to be pervasive in schools and, to the fullest extent possible, we should be working to enforce the laws that protect student survivors of sexual violence. Yet, Education Secretary Linda McMahon and the Trump administration have decided to ignore what survivors need, instead weaponizing Title IX to attack trans students,” said Shiwali Patel, senior director of education justice at the National Women’s Law Center.

title: Senate passes historic bill to regulate college sports. Its toughest test comes next.
description:
The Protect College Sports Act is halfway home.
U.S. senators on Monday overwhelmingly voted to pass legislation intended to bring regulation to an unruly industry — a historic moment in NCAA history but one expected after lawmakers advanced the bill through multiple procedural steps over the last week.
The bill, mainly authored by Republican Sens.
fullText:
The Protect College Sports Act is halfway home.

U.S. senators on Monday overwhelmingly voted to pass legislation intended to bring regulation to an unruly industry — a historic moment in NCAA history but one expected after lawmakers advanced the bill through multiple procedural steps over the last week.

The bill, mainly authored by Republican Sens. Ted Cruz and Eric Schmitt and Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell, garnered 77 supporting votes in the 100-member chamber — a considerable margin in such a divided Congress and a result that now sends the legislation toward the House of Representatives in an authoritative way.

"We wanted a big bipartisan vote," Cruz said earlier Monday. "We got a big bipartisan vote."

But as supportive lawmakers celebrate their thundering victory, a question continues to loom: Will the legislation pass the House?

"That bill is dead," said one Democratic House staff member.

"We have no intention to return to take up this bill before the midterm elections," said another.

Even the most ardent supporters of the legislation believe a stiff challenge awaits in the 435-member House, which historically operates in a more unpredictable manner because of its sheer size, diverse makeup and clashing cultural and geographic beliefs — even among those within the same party. Unlike the Senate's 60-vote procedural voting threshold to bypass the chamber's filibuster, House legislation only needs a simple majority for passage.

In the House, Republicans hold a four-vote margin — for now.

There are landmines that threaten to tank the bill across the landscape of the lower chamber of Congress. That starts with the elections themselves on Nov. 3.

House members are not scheduled to return until Nov. 9, after the midterm elections, where many projections have Republicans losing control of the chamber.

Cruz says he's held "extensive conversations" with House Speaker Mike Johnson and Cruz continues to believe that the House will return before the elections to take up the Act. "The House can pass this in one day," Cruz said earlier Monday.

Despite Cruz's confidence, House officials — even Johnson himself earlier this month — contend that will not happen.

Before the new Congress takes over in January, a five-week House work session (Nov. 9-Dec. 17) is scheduled, often referred to as the "lame-duck" period. The period is known for its unpredictability as outgoing lawmakers — those who did not seek re-election or lost their bid — may vote in more of an unusual manner.

If the Democrats win back the House during the midterm elections, will they vote for legislation in a chamber that, in just two months, they will control?

Either way, the fact that the House doesn't plan to return before the elections means that, in likely some way, the results will impact membership views and perhaps voting trends. It creates more unpredictability in a chamber that swims in volatility.

This is no normal bill, either.

The legislation would grant the NCAA an antitrust exemption — a rarity! — to limit athlete transfer movement (one transfer without penalty); standardize a five-year eligibility policy; more strictly regulate a new, increased player revenue-share cap; create an agent registry with a maximum 5% fee.

The bill also paves the way for Football Bowl Subdivision conferences to pool their media rights; features an anti-conference expansion section; and prevents coaches, who have left before a team's season ends, from performing duties at another university (the so-called Lane Kiffin Rule).

For years, perhaps even decades, animosity and dissension has existed between the upper (Senate) and lower chamber (House) of Congress.

That may be stronger now than ever.

"The House doesn't just take bills because they have passed the Senate," said one congressional expert who's spent years on Capitol Hill. "This is personal. Ted Cruz is holding up several House bills in the Senate."

It's personal for another reason: House lawmakers poured years and resources into a separate college sports bill, the House-authored SCORE Act, which failed to gain the necessary votes in the chamber twice last fall and again this past spring. The SCORE Act, friendlier to the NCAA and authored by Republicans, did not even garner enough Republican support.

The legislation even struggled to advance through the first step in the House's bill approval process, which is passage through the House Rules Committee, made up of Republican and Democrat lawmakers.

Many House members, comparing the two bills side by side, want the PCSA revised with components that existed within the SCORE Act, including most notably a provision that prevents college athletes from being deemed employees.

There are plenty more problematic issues for House members, such as the legislation offering athletes a pathway to private right-of-action (Republicans traditionally don't support such a concept); those against heavy government involvement in any industry; uncertain funding around historically Black colleges; and a conference expansion provision that's flustered several state delegations whose universities hope to, one day, move conferences — Florida's most of all.

Last year, the 58-member House Congressional Black Caucus — a group of left-leaning Democrats — stood against the SCORE Act. Also last year: Some of the 30-plus member House Freedom Caucus — right-wing Republicans — did the same.

This is a good example of an issue — regulating college sports — that has created divide within parties and generated strange bedfellows.

The many factions and groups in a 435-member chamber often complicate any voting process.

Already, the CBC has publicly opposed the Protect College Sports Act. Freedom Caucus members are expected to raise key concerns, including possibly wanting a limitation on foreign athletes permitted on college rosters.

Some Freedom Caucus and CBC members are on the all-powerful House Rules Committee, a group that must approve any legislation for it to reach the floor for a vote. There is a more unconventional way for legislation to reach the House floor, such as a suspension of the rules, which Speaker Johnson can call. However, a suspension bill vote must gain two-thirds majority for passage — a difficult task.

That doesn't mention House-induced revisions and amendments to the bill that would then need Senate support.

Buckle up for several more weeks of lobbying, stumping and — unfortunately — political ad campaigns.

title: Jadarian Price’s fumble issues are not new
description: Jadarian Price’s fumbles to start his NFL career are a continuation of a college concern.
fullText:
The Seattle Seahawks have been blessed with tremendous ball security from their main running backs over the past few seasons. Kenneth Walker III never lost a fumble with the Seahawks and only had one career fumble on an actual run play, while Zach Charbonnet's next fumble will be his first.

Walker is on another team (and looking like a viable Offensive Player of the Year candidate) while Charbonnet isn't back for at least another two weeks. The Seahawks are relying on Jadarian Price to be an immediate contributor as a first-round pick. He's shown some flashes of explosive runs and an ability to be a receiving threat out of the backfield, so there's been a good helping of promising plays.

He's also put the ball on the ground twice in as many weeks.

.@ZavenCollins liked what he saw 😳#SEAvsAZ | 📺 FOX pic.twitter.com/QHufimdBab

FUMBLE 🚨@SEAvsWAS on FOX/FOX One
Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/RNgk2tQRjX

The second fumble was enough for the Seahawks to bench him until the two-minute drill of the first half of their 33-31 loss to the Washington Commanders. It might seem like tough love, but Price is a rookie and he doesn't have the same leeway as more established running backs.

"I think just as a team, if we turn the ball over, it's not good business," Mike Macdonald said after the game. "So, when you come back after the initial fumble, we decide to calm it down and bring it back after the half. He's gonna be fine. He's gonna figure it out, he'll be fine."

"I made a mistake," Price said. "Just got to deal with the consequences."

Price only carried the ball two more times and had just six total touches for 21 yards. It was a day in which the Seahawks generated almost nothing on the ground, so it wasn't like Emanuel Wilson or George Holani were significantly better.

But the fumbling for Price is not a new issue. It was brought up in his final season at Notre Dame, in which he fumbled three times (losing two) on just 113 carries. All of his fumbles last year were inside the opposition 10, with C.J. Carr preventing a hat trick of red zone turnovers. That may or may not be why Seattle has been hesitant to give him the ball in goal-to-go situations.

Adding his 12 games in his final Notre Dame season, Price has five fumbles in 15 games. That's five fumbles over 141 carries, or one on every 28 attempts. In effect, that's two games worth of carries for Price. James Cook of the Buffalo Bills led all running backs in the NFL with six fumbles last season, except that's on 309 carries and he did a little thing called leading the league in rushing yards. Price hasn't quite built up that sort of equity to where the fumbles are a minor story due to terrific productivity.

This is not an indictment of the pick or an indication that this is who Price will always be. But for someone who was not the primary back at Notre Dame and hasn't even had the bulk of the carries as a pro, this is a legitimate concern until he fixes it. I trust that Price will be able to work on this as he develops, but it's a weakness in his game that opposition defenses are going to relentlessly attack. And this, never mind any pass protection concerns, might affect his workload until he earns the trust of the coaching staff.

title: Giants manager Tony Vitello ends rough first season with MLB-high seventh ejection
description: The Giants took a big step backward in their first year under the former college coach.
fullText:
Tony Vitello's first season as an MLB manager ended a few innings earlier than expected.

The San Francisco Giants manager was ejected in the third inning of his team's season finale against the Los Angeles Dodgers on Sunday, responding irately to a check-swing call from first-base umpire Marvin Hudson. Hudson gave Vitello a quick boot, prompting Vitello to get his money's worth.

It was Vitello's seventh ejection this season, the most by any manager in MLB and the most by an National League manager since then-Cincinnati Reds manager David Bell's seven in 2023.

Tony Vitello has been ejected after arguing this check-swing call 🤬 pic.twitter.com/XcobZmbhA3

Vitello and the Giants did appear to have a point. With a 2-2 count, one out and runners on first and second, Dodgers star Mookie Betts' bat clearly went past the plate on a high fastball from Sam Hentges. It should have been strike 3, which Hentges got one pitch later on a swinging strike on another high fastball.

Check swing calls are explicitly a judgement call for umpires and are not reviewable. They are also a bit of a sore spot for the Giants in games against the Dodgers, as a 107-win Giants team had its season ended in the 2021 NLDS against the Dodgers when the umpires ruled Wilmer Flores swung at a pitch.

Vitello wasn't the manager for that game. He joined the Giants last offseason as one of MLB's most outside-the-box managerial hires in recent memory. Before 2026, Vitello had never worked in professional baseball, not even as a minor-league player. Giants president of baseball operations Buster Posey made the hire after Vitello's successful tenure as head coach at Tennessee, with the Volunteers winning the College World Series in 2024.

The Giants tasked Vitello with steering a veteran roster looking to make the playoffs for the first time since that 2021 checked-swing call. Instead, they took a massive step backwards, with the club going from an 81-81 record in 2025 under veteran MLB manager Bob Melvin to a 65-96 record under Vitello entering Sunday. They would be in last place in any other division save the historically awful AL West.

That under-performance isn't entirely Vitello's fault. An aged roster was beset by injuries, with Rafael Devers, Willy Adames, Matt Chapman, Jung Hoo Lee, Harrison Bader, Logan Webb and many more on the injured list as of Sunday, to say nothing of certain players' underperformance.

That said, Vitello also didn't exactly impress observers. The team got off to a bad start with a number of clubhouse incidents and never recovered. Vitello also caught significant flack for his handling, or lack thereof, of the Giants' Pride Night incident in June.

Vitello was a risky bet for Posey, whose own tenure hasn't been sparkling since he replaced Farhan Zaidi in 2024, which was a significant philosophical shift for the Giants. It's enough for Vitello to be considered on the hot seat for 2027, if he isn't there already.

fullText:
Western Michigan is not a program that receives much attention during the average college football season. That all changed in Week 1 this season when the team suffered a controversial, last-second loss to Michigan. The last second itself was the root of the controversy.

The NCAA admitted officials made the wrong call, but the result was not going to be overturned. Yet that didn't stop some AP Poll voters from acknowledging WMU after the result.

The Broncos had a golden opportunity Saturday against Boise State to pick up a win against arguably the best fellow G6 opponent and get into the driver's seat for a potential College Football Playoff berth.

The end result, however, was not what anyone in Kalamazoo had in mind. Boise State took home the 32-7 win in a game that was one-sided throughout.

The College Football Playoff features one spot reserved for the highest-ranked "Group of 6" team. That means any team not in the SEC, Big Ten, ACC, or Big 12. Notre Dame also has its own set of rules to qualify.

This leaves schools such as WMU and Boise State competing for that one spot. The two teams entered the week unranked, but did receive some votes in the AP Top 25 rankings. Other G6 teams receiving votes included Tulsa, North Dakota State, and James Madison.

This game essentially served as an early playoff game against two top G6 contenders. Boise State's blowout win officially bumps the team up into the top G6 spot, while Western Michigan will now try to win out, win the MAC, and hope for chaos.

Western Michigan fans may never let the loss to Michigan go, and rightfully so. That would have been a program-defining win, and some still consider it one even if the NCAA won't change the final result.

The loss does not technically eliminate WMU, but does make the road that much harder. At this point they would have to win out and win the MAC as a starting point. They would then need to hope teams like Boise State, Tulsa, North Dakota State, and James Madison, among others, suffer several ugly losses the rest of the way.

That seems like a lot to ask, especially with the way WMU looked Saturday. The focus may now shift to Michigan and how this impacts the team's CFP resume moving forward.

fullText:
The White House has banned CNN reporters from flying with Donald Trump on Air Force One for his upcoming trip to Tennessee, the network says.

Despite a judge’s order restoring CNN’s access to the White House after Trump banned the network, along with MS NOW and Politico, from covering his daily activities, reporters are still being denied entry to certain events.

In the latest roadblock, the White House announced in a Friday night note detailing the president’s schedule that CNN will not be allowed on Air Force One when Trump flies to Knoxville on Saturday for a college football game, the network reported.

CNN is part of a rotating press pool that covers White House events for major TV networks. No other outlet was listed to replace CNN in the memo, according to the network. Without a designated pooler, major networks won’t be able to televise his trip.

The network’s journalists were also stopped by a press wrangler when they tried to cover Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival at the White House for a state dinner Thursday night, the network reported.

The White House reportedly told CNN shortly before the event that it could cover the greeting ceremony but only with a photojournalist and audio technician, despite other networks being allowed to bring reporters and producers.

MS NOW also reported being blocked from the greeting ceremony. “The big question is — is this going to continue? Are we not going to be credentialed into these daily events?” MS NOW White House reporter Laura Barrón-López asked network host Symone Sanders Townsend Thursday night.

But CNN was allowed to cover Trump and Xi’s visit to the National Archives in Washington, D.C., on Friday.

The Independent has reached out to the White House and CNN for comment about the network’s coverage of Trump’s Knoxville trip.

Coverage of the White House has been spotty ever since Trump banned the three networks last Friday, calling them “fake news.”

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” the president wrote on Truth Social.

The outlets then sued to regain access to the White House, arguing the ban violated their First Amendment rights.

In an early morning ruling Thursday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate the outlets’ press badges.

But reporters were still denied entry later Thursday morning. By Thursday afternoon, reporters regained access to the White House.

The White House TV press pool had abstained from filming in solidarity with the outlets Trump banned until their access was reinstated. CBS served as the designated pooler Friday, filming Xi and Trump at the White House during the final day of his state visit.

Trump’s disdain for the mainstream press is well-documented, including his outbursts at female journalists for asking questions about the Epstein files and the Iran war. He has repeatedly targeted CNN’s Chief White House Correspondent Kaitlan Collins for “not smiling.”

But his attempt to ban several major outlets from the White House is unprecedented.

Former President Bill Clinton — who had an affair with a young staffer, Monica Lewinsky, in the 1990s that dominated the news cycle — said at the Clinton Global Initiative summit earlier this week, “There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps.

“And there's a reason we have a Constitution. Because none of us are immune from being pissed off."
